concept.name: Churning
concept.definition: Excessive trading of a customer account by a person who controls the account (typically a broker with discretion or de facto control), done for the purpose of generating commissions or fees while disregarding the customer's interests. FINRA's quantitative-suitability doctrine reaches the same conduct even without formal discretion when the broker effectively controls the account.
concept.intuition: The broker trades your account like a hamster wheel — every spin pays them a commission, whether or not any of it makes sense for you.
concept.mechanics: Proof typically requires (1) broker control over the account, (2) excessive trading measured by turnover rate, cost-to-equity ratio, and in-and-out frequency relative to the customer's objectives, and (3) scienter. Annualized turnover above roughly 6x or a cost-to-equity ratio above ~20% are common judicial benchmarks, though no single test is dispositive.
concept.formula: Turnover ratio = total purchases in period / average account equity; Cost-to-equity ratio = annualized total commissions and fees / average account equity. High values of either support (but do not alone establish) excessiveness.
concept.failure_modes: Excessiveness depends on the customer's profile: high turnover can be appropriate for an aggressive trader, so quantitative screens flag many false positives; conversely, churning via markups, fees, or zero-commission payment-for-order-flow economics can evade commission-based detection.
concept.misconceptions: Churning does not require that every trade lose money — an account can show gains while still being churned if the trading was excessive relative to its objectives; and frequent trading requested and directed by the customer is not churning because the control element is missing.
concept.example: A broker flips a retiree's $200,000 conservative account 40 times in a year, generating $18,000 in commissions on a cost-to-equity ratio near 9% per quarter; FINRA finds churning and orders restitution.
